body:
How are polymers formed?

A polymer is a large molecule formed from many smaller repeating units. The small molecules that join to form a polymer are called monomers. The process through which monomers join to form a polymer is called polymerisation.

For example, numerous ethene molecules can combine to form polyethene, a common plastic. Its long molecular chains give it properties different from those of gaseous ethene.

Polymers occur naturally as well as through manufacture. Cellulose, present in cotton and wood, and natural rubber are natural polymers. Polyethene, nylon and polyester are examples of manufactured polymers.

Important synthetic and manufactured fibres

FibreImportant characteristicCommon use
RayonRegenerated from natural cellulose, usually obtained from wood pulpClothing and furnishings
NylonStrong, elastic and lightweight fully synthetic fibreRopes, fabrics, seat belts and toothbrush bristles
PolyesterDurable and relatively resistant to wrinklingClothing and furnishings
AcrylicLightweight synthetic fibre with a wool-like feelSweaters, blankets and shawls

Rayon is often called artificial silk because of its appearance and texture. However, unlike nylon, rayon is produced by processing naturally occurring cellulose. Thus, man-made and fully synthetic do not always mean exactly the same thing.

PET, or polyethylene terephthalate, is a polyester. It is used in bottles, packaging films and synthetic textile fibres. Polyester-cotton blends combine fibres with different properties rather than producing a new type of natural fibre.

Thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics

Plastic materials can be grouped according to how they respond to heating.

PropertyThermoplasticsThermosetting plastics
Effect of heatingGenerally soften and can be reshapedDo not soften for remoulding after final setting
StructureChains can move more readily when heatedStrongly cross-linked network restricts movement
ExamplesPolyethene, PVCBakelite, melamine
UsesBags, pipes, containersElectrical switches, heat-resistant household articles

Bakelite is a thermosetting plastic used in electrical fittings because of its insulating properties and heat resistance. Melamine is another thermosetting plastic used in certain kitchenware and heat-resistant products.

PVC stands for polyvinyl chloride. It is used in pipes and electrical insulation. PTFE, commonly known by the trade name Teflon, is valued for its non-stick properties and is used in suitable cookware coatings.

Not every polymer is a hydrocarbon. PVC contains chlorine, PET contains oxygen, and nylon contains nitrogen-containing groups. The term polymer describes molecular structure, whereas hydrocarbon describes elemental composition.

Advantages and environmental limitations

Plastics are popular because many are lightweight, durable, inexpensive, easily shaped and resistant to water. Some are good electrical insulators. However, their properties differ, so a plastic suitable for an electrical switch may not be suitable for a flexible bag or a hot-food container.

Many conventional plastics decompose very slowly in the environment. Improper disposal can obstruct drains, harm animals and contribute to persistent litter. Some thermoplastics can be recycled, but actual recycling depends on the material, contamination and available collection facilities.

Synthetic fabrics may soften or melt at high temperatures. This is a safety disadvantage near flames and intense heat. Burning plastics can also release hazardous fumes; open burning of plastic waste should be avoided.

Prelims focus

  • A polymer consists of many repeating units derived from monomers.
  • Cellulose and natural rubber are natural polymers.
  • Rayon is manufactured from regenerated cellulose.
  • Nylon is a fully synthetic fibre; PET is a polyester.
  • Polyethene and PVC are thermoplastics; Bakelite and melamine are thermosetting plastics.
  • PTFE is associated with non-stick coatings.
  • Trap: A thermosetting plastic cannot ordinarily be melted and remoulded like a thermoplastic.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, ch. 3, Synthetic Fibres and Plastics, printed pp. 32–40, 2018–19 edition. NCERT, Science, Class 10, ch. 4, Carbon and its Compounds, section on carbon compounds and their applications.]

title: Polymers, Plastics and Synthetic Fibres

body:
Why do crops need additional nutrients?

Plants require mineral nutrients for growth, reproduction and other life processes. Carbon and oxygen are obtained mainly from air, hydrogen is obtained from water, and several essential mineral nutrients are absorbed through roots.

Repeated cultivation can reduce the availability of certain nutrients in soil. Farmers replenish these nutrients through suitable manures, fertilisers, crop rotation and other soil-management practices.

The 3 nutrients most prominently identified on fertiliser packages are nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K), commonly abbreviated as NPK.

What do nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium do?

  • Nitrogen: Essential for proteins and chlorophyll; strongly associated with leafy, vegetative growth.
  • Phosphorus: Important in energy transfer, root development and reproductive growth, including seed formation.
  • Potassium: Helps regulate water balance, enzyme activity and overall plant vigour, including tolerance of some stresses.

These are their commonly emphasised roles, not exclusive functions. Every nutrient participates in several plant processes. Other essential nutrients include sulphur, calcium, magnesium, iron, zinc and boron.

How do manure and chemical fertilisers differ?

Manure consists of decomposed plant and animal matter. It adds organic material, contributes nutrients and can improve the soil's structure and water-holding capacity.

Chemical fertilisers are manufactured or processed materials used to supply particular plant nutrients in relatively concentrated and measurable amounts. They can provide nutrients efficiently, but they do not ordinarily replace the full soil-conditioning role of organic matter.

FeatureOrganic manureChemical fertiliser
Typical sourceDecomposed biological wastesManufactured or processed nutrient compounds
Nutrient concentrationUsually lower and variableUsually higher and specified
Organic matterSupplies substantial organic materialGenerally supplies little organic matter
Main benefitImproves soil condition and contributes nutrientsSupplies targeted plant nutrients

Compost forms from decomposed organic waste. Vermicompost is produced with the help of earthworms. Green manure involves growing suitable plants and incorporating them into the soil to add organic material and nutrients.

Common fertilisers and NPK grades

Fertiliser grades normally give the percentage of nitrogen as N, phosphorus as P2O5 equivalent, and potassium as K2O equivalent, in that order. The latter 2 figures are standard nutrient-reporting conventions; they do not mean that the bag necessarily contains those oxides as separate ingredients.

FertiliserTypical gradeMain nutrient contribution
Urea46-0-0Nitrogen
DAP, diammonium phosphate18-46-0Nitrogen and phosphorus
MOP, muriate of potash0-0-60Potassium

Urea is a nitrogenous fertiliser. DAP provides both nitrogen and phosphorus. MOP is a common potassium fertiliser based on potassium chloride. These materials cannot be assumed to provide every nutrient needed by a crop.

Biofertilisers and responsible application

Biofertilisers contain beneficial living microorganisms that improve nutrient availability. For example, Rhizobium bacteria live in root nodules of many leguminous plants and help convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms usable in the plant-soil system. A biofertiliser is therefore not the same thing as a bag of decomposed compost.

Applying more fertiliser than a crop needs can waste resources and pollute water. Nutrient runoff can encourage excessive growth of aquatic plants and algae. Appropriate use depends on crop requirements, soil conditions and testing rather than a single fixed quantity for every field.

India's Soil Health Card programme

The Government of India launched the Soil Health Card Scheme on 19 February 2015 at Suratgarh, Rajasthan. The programme helps farmers understand soil nutrient status and obtain recommendations for suitable nutrient management.

The standard card reports 12 soil parameters: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulphur, zinc, iron, copper, manganese, boron, soil pH, electrical conductivity and organic carbon.

According to the Press Information Bureau's report dated 11 August 2026, soil-health activities continued under the government's Soil Health and Fertility programme. This is the programme status reported as of that date; numerical card-issuance totals are not required to understand its purpose.

Prelims focus

  • NPK stands for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
  • Urea is commonly graded 46-0-0; DAP is 18-46-0; MOP is 0-0-60.
  • Fertiliser grades express phosphorus and potassium as P2O5 and K2O equivalents.
  • Rhizobium is associated with nitrogen fixation in leguminous plants.
  • The Soil Health Card Scheme was launched on 19 February 2015 and reports 12 parameters.
  • Trap: Manure contributes organic matter and improves soil condition; chemical fertilisers mainly provide specified nutrients.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, ch. 1, Crop Production and Management, printed pp. 5–7, 2018–19 edition. NCERT, Science, Class 9, ch. 15, Improvement in Food Resources, section 15.1.2 on nutrient management, manure and fertilisers, 2018–19 edition. Press Information Bureau, Soil Health Card Scheme, 18 February 2025, and Soil Health and Fertility programme update, 11 August 2026, both consulted 3 November 2026. Government of India fertiliser nutrient-grade information and Southern Petrochemical Industries Corporation fertiliser product information, consulted 3 November 2026.]

body:
What is cement?

Cement is a binding material that reacts with water, sets and hardens. Ordinary Portland cement is widely used in construction because it can bind sand and stone particles together to form strong building materials.

Cement is described as a hydraulic binder because its hardening depends on chemical reactions with water. It does not become strong merely because water evaporates.

Basic materials used to make cement

The main raw materials for ordinary Portland cement include limestone and clay or other suitable mineral materials. During manufacture, these materials are heated to produce clinker. The clinker is then ground with a controlled quantity of gypsum to make cement.

Gypsum helps regulate the setting behaviour of cement. Without suitable setting control, some cement reactions would proceed too rapidly for normal construction use.

Cement, mortar and concrete are different

MaterialMain constituentsTypical purpose
CementManufactured hydraulic binderBinds other materials when mixed with water
Cement mortarCement, fine sand and waterJoining bricks and similar masonry work
ConcreteCement, sand, coarse aggregates and waterConstruction of slabs, columns and other structures

Sand is a fine aggregate. Gravel or crushed stone commonly acts as a coarse aggregate. When water is added to cement, chemical reactions called hydration reactions help the mixture set and gain strength.

Cement is an ingredient of concrete, not another name for concrete. Concrete contains cement together with water and aggregates.

Distinguishing limestone, quicklime and slaked lime

Several calcium-containing substances have similar everyday names but different chemical compositions.

SubstanceFormulaImportant fact
LimestoneCaCO3Calcium carbonate; important cement raw material
QuicklimeCaOCalcium oxide; formed when limestone is strongly heated
Slaked limeCa(OH)2Calcium hydroxide; formed when quicklime reacts with water
GypsumCaSO4·2H2OCalcium sulphate dihydrate; controls cement setting
Plaster of ParisCaSO4·0.5H2OPartly dehydrated gypsum; used for casts and moulds

Heating limestone releases carbon dioxide and produces quicklime. When quicklime reacts with water, it produces slaked lime. These changes explain why calcium carbonate, calcium oxide and calcium hydroxide must not be treated as interchangeable substances.

Gypsum and Plaster of Paris

Gypsum is calcium sulphate dihydrate. Controlled heating removes part of its water of crystallisation to form Plaster of Paris, commonly abbreviated as POP. When POP is mixed with water, it can re-form gypsum and set into a hard mass.

POP is useful for decorative moulds, casts and some medical immobilisation applications. Although both POP and cement harden when mixed with water, they are different materials with different chemical compositions and uses.

Useful properties and precautions

Cement-based construction materials can be shaped before setting and gain strength as hydration proceeds. Their performance depends on suitable constituent materials and proper handling.

Cement powder and wet cement mixtures can irritate or injure skin and eyes. They should be handled using suitable protective precautions. Cement manufacture also has environmental impacts because fuel use and the heating of limestone release carbon dioxide.

Prelims focus

  • Limestone is mainly calcium carbonate, CaCO3.
  • Quicklime is CaO; slaked lime is Ca(OH)2.
  • Gypsum is CaSO4·2H2O.
  • Plaster of Paris is CaSO4·0.5H2O.
  • Gypsum regulates the setting of ordinary Portland cement.
  • Concrete contains cement, water, sand and coarse aggregates.
  • Trap: Cement hardens through hydration, not merely through drying.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, ch. 2, Acids, Bases and Salts, sections on gypsum and Plaster of Paris, NCERT 2026–27 reprint consulted 3 November 2026. NCERT, Contemporary India – II, Class 10, ch. 6, Manufacturing Industries, section on cement industry. American Cement Association, explanations of cement manufacture and the distinction between cement and concrete, consulted 3 November 2026. American Concrete Institute, cement and gypsum reference material, consulted 3 November 2026.]
